# Conclusions
Our original research question asked how climate has affected wine production and pricing in Oregon's growing regions, and how that relationship has evolved since 1981. Taken together, our statistical and machine learning findings point to an answer that is more nuanced than either "climate change is hurting Oregon wine" or "climate change hasn't mattered yet." Both are partly true, depending on which outcome and which variety is considered/measured.

The climate trend itself is unambiguous: growing degree days, peak summer temperature, and heat stress days have all risen with tight confidence intervals over the past four decades, while the ripening-season diurnal temperature range — the day-night swing that gave Oregon's Willamette Valley its Burgundy-like suitability for Pinot Noir in the first place — has quietly narrowed. Yield, however, has not shown the damage that trend might suggest. Statewide production and yield per acre have both climbed for decades, our panel regressions found warmer conditions generally corresponding to higher yield rather than lower, and our staged SVM model could explain less than a third of yield's variance from climate and variety alone — independent, model-based confirmation that climate is not yet the dominant force behind Oregon's yield outcomes.

That resilience, though, is not evenly distributed, and this is where the machine learning phase adds something the earlier statistical work could only gesture toward. When climate information was thin (the spring-only model), the model fell back almost entirely on *which variety* it was predicting — direct evidence that variety identity, not climate, is the first-order determinant of yield outcomes at this stage of Oregon's warming. Once summer climate features entered, growing degree days emerged as the dominant driver, ahead of vapor pressure deficit, resolving the collinearity question our correlation analysis had identified. And the residual diagnostics showed that the varieties the model struggles to characterize, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Blanc, are disproportionately the state's minor plantings, meaning we have the least reliable climate-sensitivity evidence for exactly the varieties with the smallest foothold to begin with.

Red alongside the industry's own documented response, a three-decade consolidation around Pinot Noir, with Chardonnay and Riesling's statewide share collapsing over the same period Oregon's climate indicators were shifting , suggests growers have already made a consequential shift without yet seeing yield-based evidence that it was necessary. Pinot Noir shows only a moderate positive yield relationship with heat accumulation in our data, no worse than Pinot Gris and better than nothing, but the diurnal-range finding is the one piece of evidence in this report that has not yet shown up in a production number: a leading indicator for a wine-quality risk that a yield-only model, ours included, is structurally unable to see. The honest answer to our research question, then, is that Oregon's climate-wine relationship has evolved in a way that is currently invisible in the production data and will most plausibly first appear in the fruit quality of the state's most heat-sensitive, most heavily planted variety. Precisely the risk that motivated this project's proposal to build a public, climate-linked Oregon wine dataset in the first place, and precisely where we would point future work: extending this model to a quality proxy (price premium or critic-score data) rather than yield alone, and to the California and Washington comparison our original proposal envisioned but our first-phase data constraints did not yet allow.
